awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of a Skin-Covered Bone-Anchored Endoprosthetic Thumb for People with Amputation
awd_abstract_narration:
This I-Corps project focuses on the development of a skin-covered, bone-anchored, endoprosthetic thumb for people with traumatic amputation. About 6,000 people in the U.S. each year suffer a traumatic thumb amputation, resulting in the loss of about 40% of overall hand function. Existing externally worn prosthetic thumbs do not yet meet patient needs for a device that restores thumb length, form, appearance, and touch sensation. Surgical reconstruction methods such as digit transfer or bone grafting require more surgeries and sacrifices than many patients are willing to make. An endoprosthetic thumb is expected to restore more natural function, comfort, and appearance than external prostheses without the need to harvest healthy donor tissue. Consequently, patients will have better overall functional ability, employment opportunities, independence, confidence, satisfaction, and well-being. 

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of the technology. This solution is based on the development of new methods and technologies to interface living skin with artificial implant materials. The endoprosthesis are anchored to a residual bone in the thumb and covered in the patient’s own living skin using one or more skin flaps or grafts. Hand, plastic, and microvascular surgeons identify existing or new surgical methods to cover the endoprosthesis while restoring a natural appearance and some skin sensation. Development of device materials and geometries support the overlying skin to ensure that it is durable with typical use and resilient to trauma such as cuts, scrapes, and bruises. In addition to the patient user benefits described above, the endoprosthesis benefits surgeon users by providing an off-the-shelf solution to surgically reconstruct thumb length with less burden than digit transfer and bone grafting.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Intellectual Merit: This project, supported by the National Science Foundation's I-Corps program, explored the commercial potential of the EndoThumb, a first-of-its-kind implantable prosthetic thumb that is permanently anchored to a patient's residual bone and covered with the patient's own living skin. The EndoThumb is grounded in foundational research funded by NSF CAREER Award #1944001 and conducted at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. The team demonstrated in an animal model that it is feasible to completely enclose an end-of-limb prosthesis in living skin. The skin fully healed and closed over the implant, and the animals bore weight on the covered limb during normal activity. This breakthrough established the scientific basis for the EndoThumb and directly motivated its commercialization. The technology is protected by two pending U.S. patent applications.

Broader Impacts: Thumb amputation, particularly at the level of the metacarpophalangeal joint, leaves patients with extremely limited options. External prostheses are cumbersome and frequently abandoned. Surgical toe-to-thumb transfer requires 8–12 hours in the operating room and approximately one year of recovery. Available bone-anchored prostheses that protrude through the skin carry lifelong infection risks. The EndoThumb addresses all of these limitations with a permanent, integrated implant that restores thumb length, natural appearance, and skin sensation without the need to sacrifice a healthy digit.

During this I-Corps award, the team conducted 104 customer discovery interviews with hand surgeons, certified hand therapists, amputee patients, hospital value analysis committee members, insurance and coding experts, regulatory consultants, and medical device industry professionals. Interviews were conducted virtually and in-person at clinical conferences, including the annual meetings of the American Society for Surgery of the Hand and the American Society of Hand Therapists. Through this process, the team found that the technology's value extends meaningfully beyond the patient to include operational and financial benefits for hospitals and surgeons. Customer discovery interviews consistently indicated that the EndoThumb procedure has the potential to substantially reduce operating time compared to current gold-standard reconstruction surgery, as well as reduce post-surgical complications and hospital readmission rates. Interview results helped refine the go-to-market strategy. For example, sales should target specialized hand surgery centers rather than general hospitals, as hand surgery centers possess the required clinical expertise and treat a high concentration of patients who would be eligible for the EndoThumb. Because the EndoThumb serves a focused patient population, direct sales to specialized hand surgery centers may prove more effective than contracting through large medical device distributors and group purchasing organizations.

Other key insights from customer discovery include: (1) Hospital Value Analysis Committees, not individual surgeons, are the actual purchasing decision-makers, requiring a deliberate multi-stakeholder engagement strategy; (2) external thumb prostheses are widely abandoned within months of fitting, confirming a strong unmet clinical need; (3) restoring skin sensation is deeply valued by patients and therapists, but achieving this reliably will require continued technical development; (4) reimbursement coding for a novel implant of this type is a complex, multi-year process that requires early strategic planning; and (5) surgeons have concerns about the long-term durability of the skin-implant interface that need to be addressed in the EndoThumb design.

The team determined that a viable path to commercialization exists, a conditional "go" decision. Ongoing and future commercialization activities include product development, additional customer discovery, submission of patent applications, engagement with the FDA and regulatory consultants about testing requirements, and pursuit of federal small-business funding. This I-Corps experience fundamentally shifted how the team approaches commercialization, from a technology-first perspective to one centered on understanding and serving the needs of patients, clinicians, and the healthcare system. These insights are guiding every aspect of the team's path forward.
